description: Tariff deep-dive: billing state accumulation, tiered energy cost edge cases, tariff type enum coverage, and URDB JSON parser verification.

reviews.title: BillingState energy/demand accumulation: kWh, demand peaks, fixed charges, tier logic, period resets
reviews.prompt: The BillingState tracks cumulative energy consumption (kWh), peak demand (kW), fixed charges, tier crossings, and period boundary resets. This is the foundation for all cost calculations. Review the accumulation logic: (a) Per-period energy: for each tariff period (on-peak, off-peak, shoulder), verify that energy consumption is accumulated in the correct period bucket based on the current timestep's time-of-use mapping. A common bug is accumulating in the wrong period when the timestep straddles a period boundary—either the entire step goes to one period (biased) or it should be prorated. (b) Demand charge tracking: peak demand (maximum average power over a demand window, typically 15 or 30 minutes) must track the rolling window maximum, not the instantaneous power. Verify the demand window length is configurable and the rolling window correctly resets at billing period boundaries. (c) Fixed charges: daily or monthly fixed charges should be applied exactly once per period. Verify that partial periods (first/last month of simulation) are handled correctly—a simulation starting mid-month should only charge a prorated fixed fee. (d) Tier crossing: as cumulative monthly consumption crosses tier thresholds, the marginal price changes. Verify the billing state tracks which tier the consumption is currently in and that tier boundaries reset at the billing period boundary (monthly reset). (e) Net metering: if the tariff supports net metering, verify that exported energy (kWh to grid) is tracked separately from imported energy, that net metering credits apply at the correct rate (retail vs. avoided cost), and that annual true-up logic resets at the correct anniversary date. (f) Concurrent tariffs: some customers are on dual tariffs (e.g., separate tariffs for EV charging and household load). Verify that the billing state can track multiple tariffs concurrently without cross-contamination.

reviews.title: Tiered energy cost: block edge cases, zero-consumption, no below-block fees, single-block tariffs
reviews.prompt: The compute_tiered_energy_cost function must handle all edge cases correctly, as most residential tariffs are tiered. Review the tier calculation: (a) Block boundaries: verify that consumption exactly at a tier boundary falls into the correct block. If tiers are defined as 0-500 kWh (tier 1) and 500-1000 kWh (tier 2), consumption of exactly 500 kWh should fall entirely in tier 1 (typical utility convention: lower tier is inclusive of upper bound) or be split (501st kWh starts tier 2). An off-by-one where exactly 500 kWh triggers tier 2 pricing for all 500 kWh would overcharge by the tier differential times 500—a significant error. (b) Zero consumption: a billing period with zero net consumption should produce zero energy cost (not a negative cost or NaN). Fixed charges may still apply. (c) No below-block fees: verify that if the tariff has a baseline (below-block) allowance with a different rate or zero rate, the block calculation does not charge for consumption below the baseline. (d) Single-block tariff: a tariff with only one tier (flat energy charge) should compute the same cost as a flat-rate calculation. Verify no off-by-one where a single-block lookup fails. (e) Multi-block with different rates: a common test is 3 tiers with rates $0.10, $0.15, $0.20 per kWh. For consumption of 800 kWh with tier boundaries at 500 and 1000, the cost should be 500×0.10 + 300×0.15 = $95.00. Verify this arithmetic. (f) Rate components: some tariffs have separate energy and delivery charges per tier. Verify the function accumulates both components per block. (g) Time-of-use × tier interaction: some tariffs apply tier thresholds within each TOU period; others apply an aggregate monthly threshold. Verify which model is implemented and that it's consistent with the tariff specification. (h) Negative consumption (net export in a net-metering scenario): how does the tiered function handle negative kWh? It should credit at the appropriate export rate, not apply tier pricing.

reviews.title: Tariff type enum: flat, TOU, tiered, demand-charge, net-metering, time-varying export rates
reviews.prompt: The tariff type enum defines which rate structures the system can model. Missing types silently produce wrong economics for any dwelling on that rate structure. Review the enum for coverage of common residential rate structures: (a) Flat: single energy charge per kWh, constant at all times. (b) Time-of-use (TOU): different energy charges for different time periods (on-peak, off-peak, shoulder, super-off-peak). Verify support for seasonal TOU schedules (summer/winter period definitions). (c) Tiered (inclining block): energy charge increases as monthly consumption exceeds thresholds. Verify support for inclining and declining block rates. (d) Demand charge: charge based on peak power (kW) over a demand interval, in addition to or instead of energy charges. Verify support for coincident and non-coincident demand charges. (e) Net metering (NEM): exported energy credited at retail rate, avoided cost rate, or a time-varying export rate. Verify support for NEM 1.0 (retail credit), NEM 2.0 (partial retail + non-bypassable charges), and NEM 3.0 / net billing (avoided-cost export rates). (f) Time-varying export rates: export compensation varies by time of day (e.g., California's NEM 3.0 with hourly avoided cost calculator). (g) Real-time pricing: energy charge varies hourly based on wholesale market prices. (h) Critical peak pricing: extremely high rates during a limited number of event hours per year, with lower rates the rest of the time. (i) Electric vehicle rates: separate meter or TOU period for EV charging. For each missing type, assess how many US residential customers are on that rate structure to prioritize implementation. Also review the tariff dispatch logic: once a tariff type is added to the enum, is there a corresponding billing calculation branch, or does the new variant fall through to a default (wrong) calculation?

reviews.title: URDB JSON parser: test against fixtures, energyratestructure, demandratestructure, fixedchargefirstmeter
reviews.prompt: The URDB (Utility Rate Database) JSON parser converts OpenEI URDB tariff specifications into HARES tariff types. The URDB format is complex with many optional fields; the parser must correctly extract energyratestructure, demandratestructure, and fixedchargefirstmeter. Review the parser: (a) energyratestructure: this is a list of period×tier rate structures. Verify the parser extracts the correct number of periods, the correct number of tiers per period, and the correct rate values. A common URDB parsing bug is misinterpreting the period numbering (0-indexed vs. 1-indexed) or the tier structure (list of lists vs. flat list). (b) demandratestructure: similar to energy rates but applied to peak demand (kW). Verify the demand window length (typically 15, 30, or 60 minutes) is extracted and applied correctly. Some tariffs have multiple demand charge types (generation demand, distribution demand, transmission demand)—verify all are parsed. (c) fixedchargefirstmeter: monthly fixed charges. Verify the parser extracts daily and monthly fixed charges, and that it handles compound fixed charges where the daily charge depends on the month (winter/summer differential). (d) Test against URDB fixtures in tests/fixtures/urdb/: every fixture file should parse without error and produce a tariff that matches the known-good interpretation. Add a test that parses all fixtures and compares annual bills for a standard load profile against independently calculated bills (from the URDB API or a manual calculation). (e) Optional fields: URDB has many optional fields (energyweekdayschedule, energyweekendschedule, demandweekdayschedule, etc.). Verify that the parser handles the absence of these fields gracefully (e.g., a tariff with no demand charges should produce None for demand, not panic). (f) Seasonal schedules: URDB tariffs can have up to 12 monthly schedules. Verify the parser maps each month to the correct schedule index. (g) Units: URDB uses mixed units (¢/kWh, $/kW, $/month). Verify all unit conversions to HARES internal units (likely $/J and $/W). A factor-of-1000 error in energy-to-J conversion would make bills off by 3.6×.
